comments.bodyText: Ping @mrocklin : Matrix Expressions seem to be your thing. What are your thoughts on this?

Regarding 1.  Eq subclasses Expr and so will be assumed by much of sympy to be a scalar, not a Matrix.  Historically we've had to reinvent all of the Expr terms, e.g. Add -> MatAdd.  One might have to do the same with Eq -> MatEq.  _eval_Eq seems reasonable as long as it doesn't return something that is an instance of Expr.
Regarding 2.  Exprs, and MatrixExprs don't mix well.  They assume different invariants.  In particular MatrixExprs contain non-Basic as args.  MatrixElement which is an Expr but contains MatrixExprs, often has issues as a result.

Here are my thoughts:
** warning, thought spew ahead **
1. Eq and Matrices:
I actually do think there should be a MatEq, but I also think that Eq should work with matrices (both MatrixExpr and Matrix, and all its variations). I think they should do different things though. Basically there are two kinds of statements that could be thought of to represent matrix equality:

Are the expressions equal (A == B, where they are both Matrix like). This is inherently a scalar value (True or False, either they are or they're not, or it remains unevaluated).
Are the terms equival? Similar to how other matrix libraries (numpy) work with relationals, will return a matrix of True, False, or unevaluated.

The main question is, what should do what? I have some inner conflicts on this, so I'll just lay them all out. Many disagree, as I'm not actually certain on what's best.
Lots of thoughts:

Eq previously always returned a scalar, so Eq(Matrix, Matrix) and Eq(Matrix, MatrixExpr) should go for number 1.
MatrixExpr operations in the past have always been enclosed in their own types. Anything with a MatrixExpr should return a Mat* thing.
Mat* in the past have always referred to operations that were done on matrices. Since MatEq should be a matrix operation, it should be attempting to return a matrix of Eq-like things, and remain unevaluated if it can't.
Some MatrixExpr types actually do evaluate to scalars (or at least 1 x 1 matrices). Do we treat these as scalars? Should this work with Eq or MatEq?
Elementwise will never work between MatrixExpr types. They are either algebraically equivalent, or they aren't. This is a scalar value, and should be represented by a Eq.

I really am not sure how to handle this.
The main reason for having an elementwise instead of just an overall Eq is because if we support Eq, other relationals should be added as well. There are other interpretations for these as well, but most will assume it's elementwise (what other matrix libraries do). I do think it would be neat to support linear matrix inequalities though, but this is probably outside scope.
2. Eq and MatrixElement:
So subclassing MatrixElement from Symbol doesn't make technical sense. Still, I think more support for this type of operation needs to be looked into.  MatrixElements are inherently scalar, symbolic references to a the value held in a single element of a matrix. I should be able to do anything with them that I can do with a Symbol. They aren't atomic though, as both the base matrix and the indices can be expressions themselves. I'm really not sure how to handle this.  I don't have immediate need for this feature, but it really should be supported.

Latest situation in master:
>>> Eq(A, B)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "./sympy/core/relational.py", line 384, in __new__
    dif = lhs - rhs
  File "./sympy/matrices/expressions/matexpr.py", line 24, in __sympifyit_wrapper
    return func(a, b)
  File "./sympy/core/decorators.py", line 132, in binary_op_wrapper
    return func(self, other)
  File "./sympy/matrices/expressions/matexpr.py", line 97, in __sub__
    return MatAdd(self, -other, check=True).doit()
  File "./sympy/matrices/expressions/matadd.py", line 49, in __new__
    validate(*args)
  File "./sympy/matrices/expressions/matadd.py", line 89, in validate
    raise ShapeError("Matrices %s and %s are not aligned"%(A, B))
sympy.matrices.common.ShapeError: Matrices A and -B are not aligned
>>> Eq(A[1,0], B[1, 0])
Eq(A[1, 0], B[1, 0])

The first should be easy to fix by defining _eval_Eq on MatExpr. It would need to unconditionally return an Equality when it cannot return a bool, to avoid the code in the Eq constructor that does lhs - rhs. The _eval_Eq would be something like
def _eval_Eq(self, other):
    if not isinstance(other, MatrixExpr:
        return False
    if self.shape != other.shape:
        return False
    if (self - other).is_ZeroMatrix:
        return True
    return Eq(self, other, evaluate=False)
Eq(A[1,0], B[1, 0]) works so we should make sure it is tested, so it doesn't break again.

Depending on how I interpret what you are saying, it is either wrong or confused (at best). Note that mathematically, in a real (or complex) context, lim f(x) as x -> a exists iff for every sequence xn with xn -> a, the sequence f(xn) converges (to the same value).

issues.title: Modular inverse for negative modulo and sign resolve
issues.bodyText:
SymPy assigns mod_inverse(a,m) the same sign as a.
Mathematically, mod m has range [0,m) for m>0 , (m,0] for m<0.
The former sign assignment is used in C/C++/Java built-in modulo operator as -2%5 returns -2.
The latter sign assignment is used in Python's built-in modulo operator as -2%5 returns 3.
>> mod_inverse(2,5)
3

>> mod_inverse(-2,5)
-3
SymPy does not find modular inverses for negative modulo (because of the m>1 check).
>> mod_inverse(2,-5)
>> mod_inverse(-2,-5)

Moreover, as checked from WA (uses the same sign as m rule)
mod_inverse(-2,+5) = 2
mod_inverse(+2,-5) = -2
mod_inverse(-2,-5) = -3

issues.title: Jupyter notebook LaTeX output breaks when processed in LaTeX, ironically
issues.bodyText:
Steps to reproduce:


Create a Jupyter notebook (named, say, mynotebook.ipynb) with this content:
import sympy as sp
sp.init_printing()
1


Convert it to LaTeX (you can remove the --execute flag if you saved the result in the notebook):
python3 -m nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --execute --to pdf



This creates the error (originating from LaTeX):
...
! LaTeX Error: Bad math environment delimiter.

See the LaTeX manual or LaTeX Companion for explanation.
Type  H <return>  for immediate help.
 ...                                              
                                                  
l.300     $$\begin{equation*}
                             1\end{equation*}$$
? 
! Emergency stop.
 ...                                              
                                                  
l.300     $$\begin{equation*}
                             1\end{equation*}$$
...

If you only convert --to latex, you'll see that this LaTeX code is generated:
...
\texttt{\color{outcolor}Out[{\color{outcolor}1}]:}
    
    $$\begin{equation*}1\end{equation*}$$
...
The reason for this error message is that the equation* environment is meant to be used in text mode, but sandwiching the whole thing between $$ switches to math mode.
In this case the $$ should simply be removed, but a general solution to this problem might be more involved.

Please note that using a math environment (like equation*) is a step into the wrong direction, see #15329.
I've created PR #15625 to fix this.

Yeah, I guess such a test would be good.
You could also consider moving the notebooks from the examples/ directory to your docs.
This way they could be automatically executed (using my little nbsphinx extension) whenever the documentation is built. You could then make building the docs part of the CI tests.
And when generating the PDF of the docs, this error here would be spotted.

Actually we don't even ship the notebooks, the main reason being that we don't have automated testing for them. So I agree moving them to the docs and rendering them as part of the tests would be good.

I was pointed to https://github.com/computationalmodelling/nbval as a way to test the output of notebooks (apparently it's also not hard to do manually, see https://twitter.com/SylvainCorlay/status/1074744629512286215).

There was discussion some time back about where notebooks belong. This was created but never populated:
https://github.com/sympy/sympy-notebooks
An then this was created separately:
https://github.com/sympy/quantum_notebooks
One key thing is that we wouldn't want to commit notebooks with outputs or have to host image binaries in the main sympy directory.
It is easy enough to execute the notebooks on travis with something like:
jupyter nbconvert --debug --ExecutePreprocessor.enabled=True --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=300 --to=html nb.ipynb

Yeah but the problem with just executing the notebooks is that it doesn't check that the output stays the same. Ideally it would also test the output, like we do for doctests.
I agree if a notebook has any kind of image output it should note be stored in this repo.
Yes, sure. The command I posted is better than not running them at all, and checking the output is even better. The former is pretty low overhead to setup as an initial "test".

The error in this issue occurred during the LaTeX run, so the nbconvert command would have to use --to=pdf to detect this error.
I guess nbval doesn't help in this case, because it looks at the output in the notebook file as opposed to the resulting HTML/LaTeX/PDF file, right?
My main question about the notebooks is: do you want their contents to be part of the documentation or not?
If yes, you should consider using nbsphinx.
If not, but you want to use them as regression tests, you should consider using nbval.
Theoretically, you could also do both. But I guess the content of the notebooks should very much depend on whether they are used as part of the user documentation or as part of the automated tests.

No, we would have to test that separately. My point about nbval is that if we have rendered notebooks in the docs, then we should actually test the output of the notebook cells, the same as we do with doctests. The point of doctests isn't to be regression tests (we have normal tests for that). They should rather be thought of as documentation that happens to be tested. It tests that the output of the documentation examples is actually what it says that it is, and if changes, we are aware of it and it gets updated. Sometimes this catches actual regressions as well, but that's not the point of it. I see something like nbval filling the same role as doctests for example notebooks.

Currently, SymPy does not have any control systems library.
There have been some PRs, but I see they are stalled for years now.

import sympy as sp

# Define symbols
T1, T2, Q, Ta = sp.symbols('T1 T2 Q T_a')
R1, R2, C1, C2 = sp.symbols('R1 R2 C1 C2')

# Define state variables and input

U = sp.Matrix([Q, Ta])

issues.title: How should LaTeX parser parse a(b+c)
issues.bodyText:
We have arrived to this problem in #19466 (comment) that it's ambiguous to parse a(b+c) because it can either be a multiplication between a and b+c or a function named a applied to b+c.
I don't think that we can cope with this ambiguity, so I had a thought of providing an user option to define the behavior to prefer function or multiplication if such conflicts occur, such as a whole dictionary of flags like {'a' : True}.
but I don't even know that this idea is easy to implement with antlr, or if this brings some other ambiguity.

comments.bodyText: Can the user pass in a set of names that should be defined? If so, then if a is a Symbol it should be a multiplication but if it is a Function it should be a function application. We could also use some heuristics, like if there is a space after a, it should be a multiplication. There can also be a flag to force it to always choose the ambiguity one way or another when the heuristics fail.

Since I ran into this issue even with the Lark-based parser, I think we should resume discussion on this topic.
One thing that Lark can do that ANTLR cannot do is to mark an expression as ambiguous, and return all the possible interpretations. For example,
>>> latex_str = '\\left( a b \\right)^{x \\left( c + d \\right)}'
>>> expr = parse_latex_lark(latex_str)
>>> print(expr2)
Tree('_ambig', [(a*b)**x(c + d), (a*b)**(x*(c + d))])
It's a little hard to tell here but the first case considers x as a function name, and the second example considers it as a variable.

One idea I had was to create a SymPy class that stores all the possible interpretations and then the user can choose whichever one they want, but I'm open to other suggestions too.
In particular, I like this idea:

There can also be a flag to force it to always choose the ambiguity one way or another when the heuristics fail.

I'm not a big fan of adding heuristics because that would be very tricky (to do in Lark, at least) and still not 100% accurate.

My opinion is that we can raise errors when the parser intrinsically encounters _ambig, usually, an error is enough to give user feedback that there is some ambiguity, and it can notify users to some explicit parenthesis or operators can escape any ambiuity.
And also, other options are completely disabling user-definable functions or restricting them, if there is not much usage about them. The best is to eliminate the ambiguity from the design of the grammar.

My opinion is that we can raise errors when the parser intrinsically encounters _ambig

I entertained this option, but the issue is with functions which take only one argument. Let's say I have something like \int f(x) dx. It's obvious to us that the only correct interpretation of f(x) in this case is an applied function, but the parser still chokes on this. Indeed, we see
>>> parse_latex_lark(r"\int f(x) dx")
Tree('_ambig', [Integral(f(x), x), Integral(f*x, x)])
Here's another example:
>>> parse_latex_lark(r"f(x) = \sin x")
Tree('_ambig', [Eq(f(x), sin(x)), Eq(f*x, sin(x))])
In essence, there is no way to disambiguate functions which take only one argument in a way that the parser will say "Yes, this is a one-argument function and not something else." This greatly hampers useability of the parser because now I can't use that integral expression and then substitute f(x) = \sin x or something for the function.

The best is to eliminate the ambiguity from the design of the grammar.

Could you elaborate on this? This is not a limitation of the grammar but the fact that a single letter followed by parentheses is an inherently ambiguous expression that we use on a daily basis. The reason we don't get confused is because we use the surrounding context to determine which is the correct interpretation. Baking this "context" into the grammar is not an easy task, if not impossible.

people would rarely or never write the multiplication as x(y), because it’s redundant than xy, so there is a possible rule to exclude that from multiplication grammar, unless it is too difficult to figure out

people would rarely or never write the multiplication as x(y), because it’s redundant than xy

While that's true, we will still run into cases where people need something like f(x + y) to be a function evaluation and Lark will flag it as an ambiguous expression. The solution you mentioned here of only using f, g, h, or more generally, a subset of symbol names for functions) will solve the problem for good, I'd say.
While I may be able to coax the LaTeX grammar into thinking that something like SYMBOL L_PAREN SYMBOL R_PAREN is a function call, it's hard to make it think that f(x + y) or f(x^2) is a function call.
If we go for the solution we were discussing in the linked discussion, the question then becomes: What should we use as a default? I'd like to get your thoughts on this matter.
While we should have a reasonable default for what counts as a function name and what counts as a variable name, I would like to mention that I am also working on adding some user customizability support to the grammar file (PR coming soon!), so having the perfect defaults isn't essential. issues.title: don't canonicalize imageset based on Float
issues.bodyText:
While writing this answer about how to get something resembling a float-version for range to work, I tried to think about how I would do this in SymPy. Although Floats present their own difficulties, there is canonicalization being done with imageset expressions that makes this even worse:
>>> a,b,c = 0.092, 0.433, 0.341
>>> a in imageset(x,a+c*x,Integers)
True
>>> a in imageset(x,b+c*x,Integers)
False  <- expected based on nature of floats
>>> b in imageset(x,b+c*x,Integers)  # this should not be expected
False <- not expected

That last result should represent an error. The reason it happens is because b is replaced with b%c:
>>> b, round(b%c,3), imageset(x,b+c*x,Integers)
(0.433, 0.092, ImageSet(Lambda(x, 0.341*x + 0.092), Integers))

So while canonicalization is OK for Rationals, it should not be done to Floats.
Working around this issue, here is a version of frange that might work for SymPy:
def frange(A, a, step, rational=None, _str=True):
    """return all values between `a` and `A` that are separated by `step`
    and that include `A`.

    EXAMPLES
    ========

    >>> frange(1, 3, .6)
    FiniteSet(1.0, 1.6, 2.2, 2.8)
    >>> frange(3, 1, .6)
    FiniteSet(1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0)
    >>> frange(1, 3, .6, rational=True)
    FiniteSet(1, 8/5, 11/5, 14/5)

    >>> a, b, c = 0.092, 0.433, 0.341
    >>> frange(a, b, c) == frange(b, a, c) == FiniteSet(0.092, 0.433)

    Input values are parsed in WYSIWYG fashion by using Rational
    equivalents of the `str` values of the input. Note the difference
    between the last example above and those below when this is
    disabled:

    >>> frange(a, b, c, _str=False)
    FiniteSet(0.092)
    >>> frange(b, a, c, _str=False)
    FiniteSet(0.433)

    The binary representations of `a` and `b` are such that the
    difference is not `c` unless the fraction corresponding to the
    `str` values is used:

    >>> b - a == c
    False
    >>> Rational(str(b)) - Rational(str(a)) == Rational(str(c))
    True
    """
    from sympy.functions.special.gamma_functions import intlike
    if A == a:
        return S.EmptySet
    v = A, a, step
    A, B, C = [Rational(str(i) if _str else i) for i in v]
    inf = min(A, B)
    sup = max(A, B)
    rv = Interval(inf, sup).intersection(
    imageset(x, A + x*C, Integers))
    if not rational and not all(intlike(i) for i in v):
        rv = rv.func(*[float(i) for i in rv])
    return rv

After checking things over, the code we have looks to me like a correct implementation of Alg 2.4.5 from [Cohen93], but I now think that Alg 2.4.5 may have an error.
Specifically, it looks like an error in its halting condition.
First, recall that we're using a column-style HNF, so I'm going to talk about the matrix
[1  12]
[0   8]
[0   5]

Alg 2.4.5 works row by row, starting from the bottom row and working upward. In each row it considers, it tries to make a pivot entry, working from right to left.

And I think you can offer such a condition, but the one in Alg 2.4.5 seems to be wrong.
I think a correct condition would be: "we've already found n pivots," whereas what the algorithm offers is: "we've already looked at n rows."

issues.title: [GSoC] Logarithm bases for `\lg` and `\log`
issues.bodyText:
Background
The ANTLR LaTeX Parser currently parsers \log as base e, and \lg as base 10. While writing the Lark Parser, I wondered how useful this is, because I've only seen \log to denote log base 10, and \lg as the binary logarithm (i.e., log base 2) in computational complexity-related things.
ANTLR cites ISO 80000-2:2019 as its reference for why \lg uses base 10.
When I asked my GSoC mentor @Upabjojr about this, he said that he too believes that \log should use base e.
History
Support for \lg was added in #23618. In that PR, the base for \log was also changed from 10 to $e$, citing the default of the LaTeX printer.
The reasoning given for using \lg to mean was

There seems to be an ISO standard https://en.m.wiktionary.org/wiki/lg#Usage_notes but it’s not widely used in English-language literature. I learned it to be base 10 in China.

But I'm not sure how much weightage we should give to the ISO standards argument, since there is also an ISO standard about typesetting math which says that symbols like e should be upright. However, almost no one in mathematics follows that convention.
Lark Parser
As of right now, I've preserved the ANTLR choice of bases in the Lark rewrite, but once again, I wanted to get the community's thoughts on what base the logarithm should use for both \log and \lg.

Description:
Currently, Xor is limited to canceling out duplicates but does not handle negations.
Changes Proposed:
Modify Xor._eval_simplify to call super()._eval_simplify.
Extend Xor to handle canceling out negations in expressions like Xor(b^~b).

This change aligns Xor with And and Or in terms of simplification behavior, ensuring consistency across logical operations.

The proposed changes adhere to the goal of minimizing automatic evaluation, as excessive automatic simplification can lead to performance issues and limit the representation of certain expressions, as discussed in the SymPy documentation.

issues.title: Sympy results are int, not Integer
issues.bodyText:
TL;DR: Since sympy.factor(1) returns sympy.Integer(1), it's inconsistent that sympy.divisors(1) (and even sympy.divisors(sympy.Integer(1))) does not return [sympy.Integer(1)], but [int(1)].
I noticed something potentially confusing that should at least be better documented, if not changed:
I was programming a function involving something along the lines of sum(divisor_sigma(n/d)) for d in divisors(n). Instead of a list of a few integers, the result was horribly long and looked like:
[..., divisor_sigma(1.0) + divisor_sigma(3.0) - 3, divisor_sigma(2.0) + divisor_sigma(4.0) - 4, ...]

Obviously, because I should have used integer division // instead of /. But on a second thought, users should have the right to expect that results of sympy functions should be sympy objects, unless told otherwise. If the result of the divisors() function was a list of elements of type sympy.Integer, then the result would have been as expected.
Now I understand well that it could be a big performance hit, in some situations, to always return unconditionally (and consistently) sympy.Integers instead of ints.
So, IMO, the best would be to provide an option to keep the current behaviour if desired (e.g., for performance reasons -- I guess there isn't any other reason?), or (which IMO should be the default -- maybe after some depreciation period), to return sympy objects as result.
If that isn't feasable / desired, then the documentation of the functions that don't return sympy objects should clearly say so (in the documentation of every instance), because IMO it's an inconsistency: For example, sympy.factor(1) returns sympy.Integer(1), so "why" doesn't sympy.divisors(1) (and even  sympy.divisors(sympy.Integer(1))) return [sympy.Integer(1)], but [int(1)]? Looking at the documentation (help()) of the two functions, nothing lets guess that it would be that way. [Yes, I know that factorint also returns a dict of int. And I understand that the result of factor() is (in general) a polynomial, even if it may happen to be just an integer. But again, isn't it inconsistent that sympy functions don't return sympy objects in general, unless otherwise mentioned?]

comments.bodyText: Things could be better documented but some functions are intended to operate with plain Python types rather than symbolic expressions. This is true of most ntheory functions and I don't think they should be changed because they are useful separately from all of sympy's symbolics. Potentially it would have made sense to have separate functions in different modules that handle this differently e.g. like having a divisor_sigma symbolic function in sympy.functions and a corresponding function for plain integers in sympy.ntheory. The flat import design of sympy where everything is imported at top-level makes this difficult though.

issues.title: Telescope hinges in Column module
Maximum axial forces and deflections in Column module, summary important points
issues.bodyText:
The column module can currently establish the axial force and deflections expressions. Alongside these expressions, plots can be made to visualize their distribution. However, there is no ability to find the exact values for the forces and displacements at important points, or their maximum.
A new function should be added to calculate the maximum forces and deflection, as is done in the beam module. An example of how the maximum moment in a beam can be calculated is as follows:
from sympy.physics.continuum_mechanics.beam import Beam
 from sympy import symbols
E, I = symbols('E, I')
b = Beam(10, E, I)
b.apply_load(5000, 2, -1)
p0, m0 = b.apply_support(0, type='fixed')
p8 = b.apply_support(8, type='roller')
b.apply_load(20000, 0, 0, end=8)
b.apply_load(50000, 10, -1)
b.solve_for_reaction_loads(p0, m0, p8)
b.max_bmoment()

(0, 233125/2)
Another function that could be added is a 'summary' of forces and deflections. This summary would look at which points along the column are of importance, the point of application of point loads and supports for example, and give values for forces and deflections at these points.

issues.title: fourier_series(constant) returns Integer instead of FourierSeries object
issues.bodyText:
fourier_series() returns an integer instead of a FourierSeries object when the input function is a constant. This breaks associated method calls.
from sympy import fourier_series, pi
from sympy.abc import x
from sympy.series.fourier import FourierSeries

s = fourier_series(3, (x, -pi, pi))

print(type(s))            # <class 'sympy.core.numbers.Integer'> — expected FourierSeries

s.truncate()              # AttributeError: 'Integer' object has no attribute 'truncate'
s.shift(1)                # AttributeError
s.scale(5)                # AttributeError
Also the docstring for fourier_series() states the return type is FourierSeries, which is violated for constant inputs.
Environment
Tested on SymPy 1.14.0

issues.bodyText:
Hi everyone,
I am a beginner contributing to open source for the first time. I have been analyzing the heuristic GCD algorithm (heuristicgcd.py) to see if we can optimize how the evaluation point (x) is selected.
Currently, (x) is chosen dynamically based on the max norm and trailing/leading coefficients:
f_norm = f.max_norm()
g_norm = g.max_norm()

B = domain(2 * min(f_norm, g_norm) + 29)

x = max(
    min(B, 99 * domain.sqrt(B)),
    2 * min(f_norm // abs(f.LC), g_norm // abs(g.LC)) + 4
)
Phase 1: Data Collection & Insights
To understand the baseline, I randomly generated over 100,000 polynomial pairs with constraints max_degree = 30 and max_coefficient = 100,000. I discarded data points where the actual minimum (x) required for a correct result (min_x) exceeded 30.
Here are the key insights from my data visualization:
1. Maximum Coefficient vs. min_x


Observation: Larger maximum coefficients increase the probability of needing a higher value for (x).
Insight: The average min_x remains remarkably low across the dataset. This suggests that very few polynomial pairs actually require a high evaluation bound.

2. Sign Balance vs. min_x


Observation: When the number of positive and negative coefficients approaches equality (ratios around 0.0, 0.5, and 1.0), min_x spikes dramatically. This can likely be explained by the constructive and destructive nature of polynomial evaluation.
Insight: For polynomial pairs with large coefficients combined with a sign balance ratio close to 0.5, we might want to bypass the heuristic model entirely and fall back to another method.


Phase 2: Testing & Benchmarking
I customized the core code to anchor (x) to fixed values and benchmarked them using 10,000 polynomial pairs (max_degree = 30, max_coefficient = 100,000).

While testing these fixed thresholds, the univariate tests passed, but the multivariate tests failed. To address this, I introduced a tier-based (x) determination scheme which successfully passed all existing internal tests.
Initial vs. Custom Tier Benchmarks:
=== ORIGINAL SYMPY ===
WORKLOAD 1 (Moderate Scale): Avg 0.26733 ms per call
WORKLOAD 2 (Heavy 90-Digit): Avg 0.95882 ms per call

=== MY MODIFIED CODE ===
WORKLOAD 1 (Moderate Scale): Avg 0.11824 ms per call

The Dilemma: While the initial run showed performance boosts, subsequent randomized benchmark comparisons fluctuated—sometimes my tier method was faster, other times the original implementation performed better.
To achieve more consistent performance, I adjusted the tiered ranges based on the size of the maximum coefficient:

max_coeff < 10^10 (\rightarrow x = 1,000)
max_coeff < 10^20 (\rightarrow x = 100,000)

This approach yielded highly stable results:

Custom Tiers Total Time: ~0.08 to 0.16 seconds
Standard Scaling Total Time: ~0.83 to 0.92 seconds


Phase 3: Workflow Integration
To leverage the sign-balance insight, I believe a preprocessing step should occur before the inner GCD function is invoked. Looking through the codebase, _gcd looks like the primary entry point:
def _gcd(self, other: PolyElement[Er]) -> tuple[PolyElement[Er], PolyElement[Er], PolyElement[Er]]:
    ring = self.ring

    if ring.domain.is_QQ:
        return self._gcd_QQ(other)
    elif ring.domain.is_ZZ:
        return self._gcd_ZZ(other)
    else:  # TODO: don't use dense representation (port PRS algorithms)
        return ring.dmp_inner_gcd(self, other)
Questions for Maintainers


Scope of Optimization: Is there a viable architectural scope for changing how $x$ is selected here? Do you think implementing a structured, tier-based evaluation point selection will provide a reliable optimization for SymPy's performance?

Polynomial Data Generator: It appears SymPy doesn't have an internal polynomial data generator specifically tailored for analyzing core GCD algorithms under variable constraints. I have built a custom data generator for this analysis—would the community find value in adding this tool to the testing suite?
